items.question: Can a stronger system prompt replace server-side authorization?
items.answer: No. A prompt can describe intended behavior, but it is not an enforcement boundary. Authorization must be checked by the server for the authenticated actor and requested resource, with validation and auditability outside the model.
items.trap: The prompt is still part of a probabilistic interaction and may be influenced by untrusted content. Treating it as a security control creates a direct path to unauthorized disclosure or action.

items.question: If a schema change is backward-compatible for ordinary clients, is it automatically safe for an AI client?
items.answer: No. The schema is only one part of behavior. Test refusals, missing evidence, unknown values, semantic invariants, rendering or execution allowlists, and model changes. Version contracts and deploy readers before writers for breaking changes.
items.trap: A model may change how it fills optional fields or reacts to new values even when the transport contract still parses.

items.question: If a response conforms to a JSON Schema, is it safe and factually correct?
items.answer: No. Schema-constrained output addresses structure, not truth, permissions, semantic correctness, refusals, transport failures, or whether a value is safe to render or execute. Validate domain invariants and apply policy after parsing.
items.trap: Structural validity is weaker than semantic validity. A perfectly valid enum or string can still be false, dangerous, unauthorized, or based on insufficient evidence.

items.question: Does putting a policy document in the context make it authoritative to the model?
items.answer: No. It makes the text available as context, not trusted or binding. The application must separate instructions from untrusted data, control what is retrieved, and enforce policy in code or authorization systems.
items.trap: Availability is not authority. Retrieved text can be stale, irrelevant, malicious, or simply misunderstood, and it competes with other context for the model's attention and limit.

items.question: If the same prompt produced the same answer in your test, can you treat the answer as deterministic business logic?
items.answer: No. A repeatable sample does not make generated text a trusted rule. Keep authorization, validation, invariants, and side effects in deterministic application code; use the model for bounded interpretation or generation and evaluate it on representative cases.
items.trap: The naive answer confuses an observed output with a guarantee. Fluent or repeatable output can still be false or change under different context, sampling, or model behavior.

items.question: What is the trap in estimating token cost live?
items.answer: Forgetting to state assumptions and cache effects, which makes the number look precise but wrong.
items.trap: Guessing a number without showing the multiplication.

items.question: The answers are stale because the model lacks our data. Is fine-tuning the fix?
items.answer: No: fine-tuning adapts behavior, not facts. Bring current data through retrieval, and fine-tune only for stable style, format, or narrow tasks where it beats prompting on the eval set.
items.trap: Teaching facts via weights is expensive, goes stale again, and does not replace retrieval.

items.question: The demo works. Is that enough to ship the GenAI feature?
items.answer: No: ship with an eval set from real usage, a deterministic fallback, visible refusal states, and a cost and latency budget per task.
items.trap: A demo proves the happy path; the product is defined by its failure modes and by what happens when the model is wrong.

items.question: What breaks prompt caching silently?
items.answer: Editing the top of the system prompt, which invalidates every cached prefix downstream.
items.trap: Thinking caching works better with higher temperature.

items.question: Is cutting the prompt in half the fastest way to make an AI feature feel faster?
items.answer: Usually not: generation dominates. Cutting output roughly in half cuts latency roughly in half; cutting input may buy 1-5%. Stream first, then reduce requests and output.
items.trap: Cost talk focuses on input tokens, but perceived latency lives on the output side and in waiting, not reading.

items.question: Semantic caching raised the hit ratio, so quality is fine?
items.answer: No: false-positive hits serve wrong answers and inflate hit ratio; track recall and sample the hits.
items.trap: In a cache, a wrong hit is invisible — unlike a miss.

mcqs.question: What does structured output primarily guarantee when supported by the provider?
options: That the result follows the supported schema
That a tool has already executed
mcqs.explanation: Schema-constrained output addresses structural adherence. It does not prove facts, permissions, or execution. The plausible distractor is truth: valid fields can still contain incorrect or unsafe values.

mcqs.question: What do temperature and top-p control?
options: The size of the context window
Sampling randomness; lower values make outputs more deterministic
The number of tools an agent can call
mcqs.explanation: They are sampling parameters: lowering them narrows randomness and stabilises outputs.

mcqs.question: Which risk is introduced by sending retrieved documents in the same chat turn?
options: The documents can contain instructions that hijack behaviour (indirect prompt injection)
The context window grows unbounded in pricing only
mcqs.explanation: Retrieved text is untrusted input and a known injection vector, part of LLM fundamentals security awareness.

mcqs.question: Users report that an AI answer feels slow. Which change most directly reduces perceived waiting?
options: Stream the response so users read while tokens generate
Raise max tokens so the answer arrives complete in one shot
Move the model call to a nightly batch job
Add more few-shot examples to the system prompt
mcqs.explanation: Streaming cuts perceived waiting to about a second; generation is the slowest step, so more output tokens make it slower, and more input rarely compensates.

mcqs.question: What does the context window limit?
options: How many requests per day you can send
How large the model weights are
How many tools an agent may use
How much prompt and generated text the model can consider in one call
mcqs.explanation: The window bounds input plus output tokens for a single call.

mcqs.question: Roughly how many tokens per day does 100K users times 10 interactions of about 2K tokens give?
mcqs.explanation: The estimation used in the field guide interview material: 100K times 10 times 2K equals 2B tokens per day.

mcqs.question: Which lever reduces both cost and latency for a chatbot with a long static system prompt?
options: Cache the stable prefix and keep the volatile user turn last
mcqs.explanation: Prompt caching rewards stable prefixes; restructuring the prompt makes cache hits likely.

mcqs.question: What does a model knowledge cutoff force you to design for?
options: Freshness through retrieval or tools for anything newer than the cutoff
mcqs.explanation: The model cannot know post-cutoff facts, so freshness has to enter through context or tools.

mcqs.question: Which output approach is best when downstream code must parse the answer reliably?
options: Structured output validated against a JSON schema
mcqs.explanation: Structured outputs with schemas give typed, consistent responses that fail loudly on drift.

mcqs.question: What is few-shot prompting?
options: Sending only one token at a time
Including worked examples of the desired input-output mapping in the prompt
mcqs.explanation: Few-shot means demonstrating the task with examples inside the prompt.

mcqs.question: Which counts as a hallucination in the strict sense?
options: A confident statement unsupported by the provided context or the model's knowledge
mcqs.explanation: Hallucination is unsupported generation presented with confidence.

mcqs.question: Why separate system prompts from user prompts?
options: Roles shape behaviour and let instructions evolve independently of user input
mcqs.explanation: Role separation is how the model weights instruction classes and how teams tune behaviour safely.

scenarios.prompt: A JSON summary endpoint works in demos but fails randomly in production: the model sometimes wraps the JSON in markdown or adds commentary.

code.code:
resp = client.chat(model=MODEL, temperature=1.2,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Summarize as JSON: {text}"}])
data = json.loads(resp.text)

scenarios.modelAnswer: Ask for structured output against a JSON schema instead of parsing free text; the model API enforces the shape. Lower temperature for extraction tasks. Validate the parsed payload anyway and treat violations as a typed error with retry (once) and a logged trace. Keep the schema minimal and version it, because schema changes are breaking changes for clients.
rubric: Validates output and handles violations explicitly
Versions the schema or notes compatibility

scenarios.prompt: A product lead asks whether to serve a chatbot to 200K daily users on a frontier model. Each user sends 8 messages of about 1.5K tokens. Walk the cost reasoning.

code.code:
users = 200_000
messages = 8
tokens_per_message = 1_500
daily_tokens = users * messages * tokens_per_message

scenarios.modelAnswer: Daily volume is 2.4B tokens before caching. Price each candidate model per million tokens and compare: the frontier model may cost multiples of a smaller model for the same traffic. Then apply levers: cache stable prefixes to cut input tokens, route simple turns to a small model, batch non-interactive work, and measure quality per dollar with an eval set instead of assuming the biggest model wins. Report the estimate as a range and state assumptions (tokens per message, cache hit ratio) because the interviewer is testing the reasoning, not the arithmetic.
rubric: Computes daily token volume from the given figures
Converts tokens to currency with per-model pricing
Names cost levers: caching, routing, batching
Anchors the decision in measured quality, not assumptions

scenarios.prompt: A support assistant with a 12K-token system prompt shows high latency and high cost. The prompt is rewritten in place several times a week.

code.code:
system_prompt = load_prompt("support_v3.txt")  # edited weekly
messages = [{"role": "system", "content": system_prompt}, *history, user]

scenarios.modelAnswer: First measure: cache hit ratio and time to first token. Restructure so the stable part of the prompt comes first and the volatile turns last, keeping edits append-only where possible to preserve prefix cache hits. Move rarely changing reference material into retrieval instead of the static prompt. If quality allows, distil the prompt to its behavioural core and consider a smaller model for simple intents. Report cost per conversation and p95 latency before and after.
rubric: Measures cache behaviour and latency first
Reorders the prompt for stable prefixes
Moves static reference material out of the prompt
Reports cost and latency metrics before and after

scenarios.prompt: A team wants to add an AI summary button to an existing dashboard. Their plan: send the whole dashboard JSON to the biggest model, render the returned text as HTML, and retry until it parses. Review the plan before it ships.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Rework the plan around failure, not the happy path. Scope: send only the data the summary needs, and ask for structured output validated at the boundary instead of retrying prose until it parses. Safety: render model output as text or through a constrained schema, never as raw HTML. Reliability: define the failure path — a deterministic fallback (top movers computed in code) and a visible empty state when the model refuses or errors. Quality: build an eval set from real dashboards with the points a good summary must hit, and gate prompt and model changes on it. Budget: cost and latency per summary, with the stable prefix cached. And question the premise: computed metrics may serve users better than generated prose.
rubric: Replaces free text with parse retries by structured output validated at the boundary
Refuses to render model output as raw HTML and treats generated content as untrusted
Defines a deterministic fallback and visible failure states
Adds an eval set from real data and a per-task cost and latency budget
